name: Fall of Constantinople
info: The Ottoman army under Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople for 53 days and took the Byzantine capital on 29 May 1453, after which the city was sacked and became the Ottoman capital; the fate of Emperor Constantine XI is unknown.

facts.date: Siege of 53 days from 6 April to 29 May 1453; the city was taken on 29 May
facts.place: Constantinople, now Istanbul, on the Bosphorus; the fighting centred on the Theodosian land walls, especially the Mesoteichion and the Blachernae district, and on the Golden Horn
facts.sides: The Byzantine Empire under Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos, with Genoese, Venetian and other foreign help: about 7,000 men, 2,000 of them foreigners by one count, and under 8,000 by Sphrantzes' census. The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mehmed II: some 50,000 to 80,000 men by recent studies, against 160,000 to 300,000 in Western witnesses.
facts.outcome: The Ottomans took the city after a final assault on 29 May. It was looted for part of three days, many of its people were killed or enslaved, and Mehmed made it his capital. Constantine XI's fate is unknown.

t: A much smaller defending force of foreigners and citizens held about 20 km of walls against a much larger Ottoman army and its cannon, and no relief from Western Europe arrived in time.
The sack was severe. Thousands were killed and, by one count, around 30,000 people were enslaved; Mehmed ordered the looting stopped and issued a proclamation to those who had hidden or fled.
Many modern historians treat the fall as the end of the medieval period, and the capture of the last Roman capital as the end of the Roman Empire.
dyk: On 22 April Mehmed had ships hauled on greased logs across the hill at Galata into the Golden Horn, bypassing the chain across its mouth that the defenders had counted on to keep Ottoman ships out.
ev: Mehmed II builds the fortress of Rumeli Hisari on the Bosphorus, and Constantine XI declares church union valid on 12 December
Giovanni Giustiniani arrives in January with about 700 men and is given command of the land walls
The Ottoman army encamps outside the city on 2 April and the siege begins on 6 April
Mehmed has his ships dragged into the Golden Horn on 22 April, and the fire-ship attack of 28 April fails
Ottoman mining from mid-May is met by counter-mines, and Constantine refuses Mehmed's offer of terms on 21 May
Shortly after midnight on 29 May the final assault begins, Giustiniani is wounded and the walls are overwhelmed
Looting and enslavement follow for part of three days, after which Mehmed halts them and has Hagia Sophia made a mosque
Mystras in the Morea, held by Constantine's brothers, falls to the Ottomans

sections.background:
Constantinople had been an imperial capital since 330 and in eleven centuries had been besieged many times but taken only once, in 1204 by the Fourth Crusade. The Nicaeans recaptured it from the Latins in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty, which then fended off Latins, Serbs, Bulgarians and Ottoman Turks. The Black Death killed almost half of the city's inhabitants between 1346 and 1349. By 1453 the city was a series of walled villages separated by fields, inside the fifth-century Theodosian walls, and by 1450 the empire had shrunk to a few square kilometres outside the city, the Princes' Islands and the Peloponnese.

Mehmed II succeeded his father in 1451 at the age of 19, and many European courts assumed that he would not challenge Christian hegemony in the Balkans. By early 1452 he was building a second fortress, Rumeli Hisari, across the Bosphorus from Anadolu Hisari, which gave the Ottomans control of sea traffic on the strait. Constantine XI turned to the West, but the union of the Eastern and Western churches that Pope Nicholas V wanted was bitterly opposed in Constantinople, and the court declared it valid only on 12 December 1452. The Pope had less influence over Western rulers than the Byzantines hoped, and those rulers were occupied by wars of their own. Some help came: Cardinal Isidore with 200 archers, and Giovanni Giustiniani from Genoa with 400 men, joined by 300 from Genoese Chios. A Venetian fleet was delayed until April and came too late, and seven Italian ships with about 700 men slipped away when Giustiniani arrived.
sections.forces:
The defenders numbered about 7,000, 2,000 of them foreigners. Constantine ordered a census at the end of March, and his chancellor George Sphrantzes recorded 4,773 Greeks and just 200 foreigners, with volunteers from outside, Genoese, Venetians and others from Galata, who numbered hardly as many as three thousand: under 8,000 in all to hold twelve miles of wall. Fewer than 50,000 people were living in the city. The land walls were 5.5 km, with sea walls along the Golden Horn (7 km) and the Sea of Marmara (7.5 km), and the defenders had 26 ships and a chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn. Constantine and his Greek troops held the Mesoteichion, where the river Lycus crossed the walls, and Giustiniani was first to the north and later beside him. The defenders' small cannon proved ineffective, and the recoil tended to damage their own walls.

Recent studies and Ottoman archival data give some 50,000 to 80,000 Ottoman soldiers, including 5,000 to 10,000 Janissaries and 1,500 Serbian cavalry that Đurađ Branković was obliged to supply to the sultan, and 70 cannon. Western witnesses, who tended to exaggerate, give 160,000 (Barbaro), 200,000 (Tedaldi and Sphrantzes) and 300,000 (Isidore and Leonardo of Chios). Contemporary estimates of the Ottoman fleet run from 110 ships to 430, and a modern estimate is 110. Cannon are given as 12 to 62. The best known was the bombard of Orban, a Hungarian (some say German) founder, said to throw a 600-pound (270 kg) stone ball over a mile, though it took three hours to reload.
sections.course:
Mehmed's cannon fired for weeks, but they were imprecise and slow, and the Byzantines repaired most of the damage after each shot. The Ottoman fleet under Baltoghlu could not enter the Golden Horn because of the chain, although on 20 April four Christian ships fought their way in. On 22 April Mehmed dragged his ships overland into the Golden Horn, and on 28 April a fire-ship attack on them failed. Forty Italians who swam ashore were impaled on stakes by Mehmed's order, and in retaliation the defenders executed 260 Ottoman prisoners on the walls. Frontal assaults on the land walls were costly failures. From mid-May Ottoman sappers, many of them Serbian miners, dug tunnels, and the Byzantines, with counter-mines led by Johannes Grant, intercepted them on 16, 21, 23 and 25 May. On 21 May Mehmed offered to lift the siege and let the emperor and any others leave with their possessions; Constantine offered more tribute but refused to give up the city.

The assault began shortly after midnight on Tuesday 29 May. Christian troops of the Ottoman Empire attacked first, then irregular azaps and Anatolian Turkmen, who breached the weaker Blachernae section but were pushed back, and last the elite Janissaries. Giustiniani was grievously wounded and his withdrawal caused panic. Constantine's men could not stop the Ottomans entering, and the defenders were overwhelmed at several points. The Venetians took to their ships and the Ottoman navy held the Golden Horn by midday.
sections.aftermath:
Mehmed promised his soldiers three days of plunder, but sources say he rode in on the first day and called a halt, since little remained from 1204. Meanwhile troops who broke into Hagia Sophia separated the crowd sheltering there by the price they might bring in the slave markets. Resisters were killed; Barbaro writes that the Turks "made a great slaughter of Christians" through the city. Leonard of Chios says sixty thousand Christians were captured; another count gives around 30,000 enslaved. David Nicolle says only about 4,000 Greeks died in the siege, and a Venetian Senate report says 50 noblemen and over 500 other Venetian civilians died. Philip Mansel writes of thousands of murders and rapes, and several chroniclers describe rape and enslavement.

Ottoman casualties are unknown but are believed by most historians to have been severe. When Mehmed saw the ruined city on 2 June he is reported to have wept. He then proclaimed that Christians who had avoided capture or had been ransomed could return home. He had Hagia Sophia turned into a mosque, appointed Gennadius Scholarius as patriarch, and made the city his capital. Constantine had died without an heir; his fate remains unknown and a severed head claimed to be his was nailed to a column. The sultan had the Catalan Pere Julià, his sons and the consul Joan de la Via, among others, beheaded. Doukas says Mehmed had Loukas Notaras executed after Notaras refused to give up his youngest son, a story Walter Andrew doubts.
sections.sources:
Marios Philippides and Walter Hanak list 15 eyewitness accounts, 13 Christian and 2 Turkish, and 20 contemporary non-eyewitness accounts, 13 of them Italian. The eyewitnesses include Tursun Beg on the Ottoman side, George Sphrantzes, the only Greek eyewitness, whose account is laconic, Leonard of Chios, Nicolò Barbaro and Cardinal Isidore. Among the others are the Byzantine historians Doukas, Chalkokondyles and Critobulus, Ottoman chroniclers Ashikpashazade and Neshri, and the 17th-century traveller Evliya Çelebi, who collected local traditions. Makarios Melissourgos, who augmented Sphrantzes, is called not very reliable, and Nestor Iskander's chronicle often unreliable.

Several points are disputed. Western witnesses exaggerate the Ottoman army, so recent studies lean on Ottoman records. The report that Orban's cannon collapsed after six weeks comes only from Leonard of Chios and Nestor Iskander. Barbaro says Constantine hanged himself, others that he died fighting in the streets, and his fate is unknown; later myths of his rescue have little evidence. Doukas's story of Notaras is doubted by Walter Andrew, who sees in it a story older than the conquest and a tendency to paint Muslims as morally inferior. The counts of the dead and enslaved differ between Nicolle, Leonard of Chios and the Venetian report. The claim that Mehmed founded the millet system is now considered a myth.
sections.legacy:
The fall marked the effective end of the Roman Empire, a state dating from roughly 27 BCE, and for many modern historians the end of the medieval period. Britannica says the Greek exodus to Italy marked the end of the Middle Ages and the start of the Renaissance. It is called a turning point in siege warfare, since walls that had protected the city for 800 years were overcome by Ottoman infantry with the support of cannon. Mehmed called himself Kayser-i Rum, the Caesar of the Romans.

In Western Europe the loss shocked many, and Pope Pius II argued for a new crusade while Nicholas of Cusa urged dialogue; no crusade came of Nicholas V's call. Mystras fell in 1460 and Trebizond in 1461. In the Islamic world the news was greeted with joy: Cairo was decorated and the Sharif of Mecca wrote to praise Mehmed. Legends grew, among them an eclipse on 22 May, a fog and a light about Hagia Sophia, which may have been effects of a volcanic eruption, and the Marble Emperor, but they are little supported. Greeks have considered Tuesday unlucky since 29 May 1453. The city became officially Istanbul only in 1930. In 2021 Greece's president laid a wreath at Constantine's statue at Mystras.

summary: Mehmed II's army took Constantinople on 29 May 1453 after a siege of 53 days, with defenders far fewer than the attackers. The city was plundered and many of its people killed or enslaved. It became the Ottoman capital, and the Byzantine Empire ended.
references: Steven Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople, 1453 (Cambridge University Press, 1965)
Marios Philippides, The siege and the fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Ashgate, 2011)
John R. Melville-Jones, The Siege of Constantinople 1453: Seven Contemporary Accounts (Adolf M. Hakkert, 1972)
Donald M. Nicol, The Immortal Emperor: The Life and Legend of Constantine Palaiologos, Last Emperor of the Romans (Cambridge University Press, 2002)
Roger Crowley, 1453: The Holy War for Constantinople and the Clash of Islam and the West (Hyperion, 2005)
Donald M. Nicol, The Last Centuries of Byzantium, 1261–1453 (Cambridge University Press, 1993)
notes: Dates: the siege is 6 April to 29 May (53 days) per the lead, but the article also says the Ottoman army encamped on 2 April and the sultan arrived on 5 April. I gave 6 April as the start and the encampment separately.

Numbers kept as the article gives them: defenders 'about 7,000, 2,000 foreigners' and Sphrantzes' 4,773 + 200 + under 3,000, 'under 8,000'; Ottomans 50,000-80,000 (recent) vs 160,000-300,000 (Western). Enslaved: article says 'around 30,000' in one place and Leonard of Chios 'sixty thousand' captured; both given, not reconciled. Greek dead 'about 4,000' is Nicolle's.

The article's 'Atrocities' section also has: Critobulus on Sphrantzes' family (a girl dying in the harem, a son killed by the sultan), a quotation that Mehmed had citizens 'hacked to pieces for entertainment' with no source named, and Nicolas de Nicolay's slave market. I left these out as graphic or poorly sourced; the editor may want the Sphrantzes family claim attributed, but the text is garbled in the article.
The Notaras story is told as Doukas's and doubted by Andrew, as in the article. The article also names Notaras as commander of a reserve; not used.
The article does not name the present-day country of Istanbul, so the facts omit it. 'Mehmed wept' is reported speech and I wrote 'reported'.
The 'Ottoman casualties are unknown' sentence is from the article. The 'Tuesday unlucky' and legends are Greek traditions, kept brief.

The article credits the Theodosian walls with 800 years of protection and says walls were overcome by 'Ottoman infantry with the support of gunpowder'; I wrote it as the article's own claim ('The article calls it'). A fuller reading could dispute it; the article gives no dissent.
Hagia Sophia's conversion: the article says 'Mehmed himself knocked over and trampled on the altar'; omitted as an uncorroborated detail.
